newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Twenty hurt as Burma refugees resist repatriation.
newsitem.headline: Twenty hurt as Burma refugees resist repatriation.

text.p: Some 20 people were injured on Sunday in clashes between Bangladeshi police and Burmese Moslem refugees resisting repatriation, officials said.
They said the victims included six policemen.
Police used teargas and fired rifle shots in the air after the "Rohingya" refugees turned on officials and securitymen with spears, axes and iron rods trying to foil attempts to send them home.
However, 187 Rohingyas were sent across the Naf border river under supervision of Bangladeshi repatriation officials and two representatives of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

"Police brought the situation under control at Nayapara camp in Teknaf hours after the violence started, and later put 187 members of 45 refugee families on several boats sailing across the river," one official said.
The returnees were received on the Burmese side by local immigration and UNHCR officials, he said without giving further details.
More than 250,000 Moslems, known as Rohingyas, fled to southeastern Bangladesh in early 1992 from west Burma's Arakan province, complaining of military persecution and forced labour.
Repatriation, supervised by the UNHCR began in September that year following an agreement between Dhaka and Rangoon.
Some 228,000 Rohingyas had gone back before the process was suddenly stopped on May 1, 1997, and Bangladesh blamed the Burmese immigration for not giving clearance to the home-bound refugees.
"The repatriation process resumed on Sunday after a meeting between Bangladeshi and Burmese officials in the Arakan town of Maugdaw on Saturday," one official in Teknaf said.

Meanwhile, Bangladeshi officials said more than 15,000 Rohingyas arrived in Bangladesh over the last three months in a new influx, triggered by what the refugees said were continuing military persecution and recent rise in food prices.
Police said border guards had pushed back over 2,000 newly-arrived Rohingyas but others mingled with local residents, who have striking physical and linguistic similarities with the Rohingyas.
The UNHCR said on Friday in Geneva that it had appealed to the Bangladesh government to give it access to thousands of of Burmese Moslems who have fled across the border over the past few months.

Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole told reporters many of the estimated 7,000 new refugees -- whom Bangladesh regards as economic migrants -- were being jailed or forcibly returned to Burma which some of them say they fled for political reasons.
"We are not being given access to these people," she said. "We wrote to the Bangladesh government two weeks ago asking to be given access to them but so far have received no reply.

"We believe some of them may genuinely fear persecution if they return to Myanmar (Burma). We again call on the Bangladesh government to allow us to interview these people and establish who might be deserving of UNHCR protection."
The Bangladesh government has yet to acknowledge or comment on the appeal.
